I redid the code (in [this commit](https://github.com/usradam/kaiaulu/commit/b543f09fb9f200eb26c741646cfc1233163c13f0)) so that `engagement_communication` is implemented. It takes into account `datetimetz` and `user_name_email`
```r
dt <- data.table::data.table(
    datetimetz = as.POSIXct(datetimetz, tz = "UTC"),
    user_name_email = user_name_email
```

It counts an author's message based on a rolling window of 90 days.
```r
# Order data
  data.table::setorder(dt, user_name_email, datetimetz)
  data.table::setkey(dt, user_name_email, datetimetz)

  # POSIXct is in seconds, so convert quit_lag from 90 days to seconds
  lag_seconds <- quit_lag * 86400

  # For each message, count how many messages occurred in prior 90 days
  result <- dt[, {
    
    window_start <- datetimetz - lag_seconds
    
    message_count <- dt[.SD,
                        on = .(user_name_email,
                               datetimetz >= window_start,
                               datetimetz <= datetimetz),
                        .N,
                        by = .EACHI]$N
    
    .(datetimetz = datetimetz,
      user_name_email = user_name_email,
      message_count = message_count)
    
  }, by = .(user_name_email, datetimetz)]
```
I made sure to only make use of the `data.table` package. I also compiled the package and documentation for the function so it is reflected in the commit mentioned above as well.

Hi @carlosparadis,

I looked into heterogeneous graphs in network theory to make sure the current implementation lines up with how they are defined in research. A heterogeneous graph is a network where nodes and edges can be different types. Each node is assigned exactly one type that describes what kind of entity it is, and each edge is assigned exactly one type that describes the relationship between two nodes. A graph is considered heterogeneous when there are more than two types combined across nodes and edges, which is what separates it from simpler graph types like bipartite graphs.

The implementation follows this definition. Each node has a unique name, a string type label like `"author"`, `"commit"`, or `"file"`, and a color. Each edge stores a source node, a destination node, a weight, and a string type label like `"authored"` or `"changed"`. This matches the standard structure used in the literature.

For projections, research on heterogeneous graphs typically uses something called meta-paths. A meta-path is a sequence of node and edge types that describes how two nodes are connected through multiple steps. For example, author to commit to file to commit to author is a meta-path that links two authors together if they both changed the same file. Meta-paths allow for more detailed analysis because they capture indirect relationships across multiple node types.

The current implementation uses a simpler approach. Instead of full meta-path projections, it pulls out a bipartite slice from the heterogeneous graph by filtering to one edge type at a time and then runs a standard bipartite projection on that slice. For example, projecting through the `"changed"` edge type collapses commits and produces a file co-change network where two files are connected if they were changed in the same commit. This is a well known method in the bipartite projection literature and works as a solid starting point. Supporting full meta-path projections is a natural next step as the pipeline grows.

### transform_gitlog_to_heterogeneous_network: Added node_cols Parameter

The function was updated to accept a `node_cols` parameter, a character vector of column names from the parsed git log. Only the node types whose columns are included will appear in the nodes table. Edges between node types are derived automatically based on which columns are present.

Supported columns and their node types:

| column | node type | color |
|---|---|---|
| author_name_email | author | black |
| commit_hash | commit | #afe569 |
| file_pathname | file | #f4dbb5 |

Edges are built automatically based on which node pairs are both present:

| node pair | edge type | weight | condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| author + commit | authored | 1 per unique pair | both in node_cols |
| commit + file | changed | lines added + removed | both in node_cols |
| author + file | modified | lines added + removed | both in node_cols, commit excluded |

The `"modified"` edge type collapses the two-hop author to commit to file path into a direct author-file edge. It only fires when commit nodes are excluded. When commit nodes are included, the relationship already exists through the two separate edge types.

Default behavior is unchanged. Calling the function with no arguments builds all three node types and both original edge types.

---

### graph.R: S3 Generic for Bipartite Projection

A new S3 generic `bipartite_graph_projection_v2` was added with two methods.

`bipartite_graph_projection_v2.bipartite_graph` handles graphs returned by `model_bipartite_graph`. The `mode` parameter is `TRUE` or `FALSE` selecting which node type to project onto. The projection logic is identical to the original `bipartite_graph_projection`.

`bipartite_graph_projection_v2.heterogeneous_graph` handles graphs returned by `model_heterogeneous_graph`. The `mode` parameter is a string node type label such as `"file"` or `"author"`. An additional `edge_type` parameter specifies which edge relationship to project through, such as `"changed"` or `"authored"`. The method slices the heterogeneous graph to the requested edge type, recodes the string node types to `TRUE`/`FALSE`, builds a `bipartite_graph` from the slice, and delegates to the bipartite method.

This means the user calls the same function regardless of whether they are working with a bipartite or heterogeneous graph. R dispatches to the correct method based on the class of the graph passed in.

Example usage:

```r
# From a bipartite graph
bipartite_graph_projection_v2(bipartite_net, mode = FALSE, weight_scheme_function = weight_scheme_count_deleted_nodes)

# From a heterogeneous graph
bipartite_graph_projection_v2(git_network, mode = "file", edge_type = "changed", weight_scheme_function = weight_scheme_count_deleted_nodes)
```

---

### transform_gitlog_to_entity_bipartite_network: Standardized Format

The function was rewritten to follow the same pattern used across the other updated transforms: validate input, build nodes table, build edgelist, call constructor.

Changes made:

- Input validation was added to stop early if the input is not a data.table
- A bug was fixed where `"committer-entity"` mode was using the author column instead of the committer column for the from nodes
- The mode mapping was consolidated into one block that sets `from_col`, `to_col`, `from_color`, and `to_color`. The node and edgelist building code is then the same for all four modes
- The nodes table is now built explicitly with `name`, `type`, and `color` columns. From nodes get `type = TRUE` and to nodes get `type = FALSE`
- The edgelist is now built by summing lines changed per unique from-to pair instead of counting occurrences
- `model_bipartite_graph` replaces `model_directed_graph` with `is_bipartite = TRUE`

Because the output is now a properly classed `bipartite_graph`, it works directly with `bipartite_graph_projection_v2` without any additional setup.

Hi @carlosparadis,

Based on my review of the documentation for NetworkX, SNAP, igraph, git2net, coronet, and Quanteda, here is what I found:

## NetworkX, SNAP, and igraph

NetworkX and SNAP both handle data loading and graph construction in a single step where you pass in raw data and get a graph object back with no separation between the two stages. igraph follows the same pattern in R where constructor functions like `graph_from_data_frame()` consume a data frame and return a graph object all at once.

igraph is the closest in similarity to Kaiaulu since it also uses R's S3 class system. The key difference is that igraph uses a single `igraph` class for all graph types and stores properties like directionality and bipartite membership as flags and vertex attributes on the same object. Kaiaulu instead uses separate S3 classes (`bipartite_graph`, `heterogeneous_graph`, `directed_graph`) which makes the graph type explicit and allows S3 dispatch to automatically route projection and export functions to the correct method. igraph supports bipartite graphs as a first-class feature but treats heterogeneous graphs by convention only where users manually set a type attribute and filter nodes and edges themselves.

## git2net and coronet

These are the most direct comparisons since both libraries transform software engineering data into networks. git2net separates parsing from graph construction by persisting all extracted git data to a SQLite database first since mining a repository is expensive and should only be done once. coronet takes a more structured approach with a four-part architecture where configuration, data loading, network configuration, and graph construction are each handled by separate classes.

Kaiaulu currently sits between these two approaches. The transform functions do separate data preparation from graph construction but there is no persistent intermediate layer like a database or a formal data class connecting the two. The advantage of this is simplicity. Where Kaiaulu stands apart from both libraries is heterogeneous graph support. Neither git2net nor coronet provides a native heterogeneous graph type. Kaiaulu's `model_heterogeneous_graph` with explicit string node and edge types is a more expressive abstraction for multi-type networks that neither library currently offers.

## Quanteda

Quanteda is the closest in similarity to where Kaiaulu's S3 system is heading. Quanteda defines a strict pipeline of S3 classes (`corpus` → `tokens` → `dfm`) where each class has its own dedicated set of functions following a `class_verb()` naming convention. This makes the API predictable and self-documenting since users always know what functions exist for a given object type. The core takeaway is that consistent naming conventions and per-class function sets can make a system intuitive and maintainable without requiring more complex class systems like S4 or R6.

Kaiaulu's `model_*` constructors and `bipartite_graph_projection` S3 generic are already moving in this direction.

Hi @carlosparadis,

Quanteda validated the S3 dispatch approach we're already taking. Building a type system where functions dispatch based on object class is cleaner than passing flags or doing manual class checks inside every function. That's the right direction for Kaiaulu.

The main design decision to avoid is coronet's four-class configuration pattern. Requiring users to instantiate and wire up ProjectConf, ProjectData, NetworkConf, and NetworkBuilder just to build one network creates a lot of unnecessary friction. Kaiaulu keeps configuration in YAML and passes data directly to transform functions, which is simpler and easier to follow.

git2net's SQLite intermediate layer is worth noting too. It solves the problem of reparsing git history repeatedly, but it adds a dependency and makes the pipeline less transparent. Kaiaulu's approach of keeping parsed data as in-memory data.tables is easier to debug and understand. I would not change that.

One thing worth considering going forward is making node and edge semantics more explicit in the API. igraph's fully generic model makes it easy to lose track of what your nodes and edges actually represent. Kaiaulu's type column in the edgelist already helps with that, but as the library grows, it might be worth thinking about how to surface that information more clearly for users.

## Pipeline Standardization: Gitlog and Depends

This week's work focused on finishing the standardization of both the gitlog and depends pipelines to follow a consistent four-stage architecture: transform, model graph, project, and export. The goal was to make sure every function in both pipelines uses the same patterns and constructors so that the graph type is always explicit, S3 dispatch works correctly at every stage, and callers never have to manage internal graph behavior manually.

Work found in this [commit](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/pull/375/changes/29b550d7e8a1de873a492488c4ebb2b95c221076)

### Transform Stage

Every transform function is now responsible for two things before calling a constructor: building an explicit nodes table and building an explicit edgelist table. This replaces the old pattern of passing a raw data.table to `model_directed_graph` with `is_bipartite=TRUE`, `color`, and `aggregate_duplicate` parameters that were handling node construction internally. Those parameters no longer exist on the constructors.

For the gitlog pipeline, six transform functions were standardized. `transform_gitlog_to_bipartite_network` and `transform_gitlog_to_entity_bipartite_network` build nodes from unique values in the from and to columns, assign `type=TRUE` and `type=FALSE` to distinguish node types, and aggregate edge weights by summing lines changed per unique pair before calling `model_bipartite_graph`. `transform_gitlog_to_temporal_network` and `transform_gitlog_to_entity_temporal_network` follow the same node-building pattern but do not aggregate the edgelist, preserving one row per git log entry so that `temporal_graph_projection` has individual timestamps per edge to work with. A bug was also fixed in `transform_gitlog_to_entity_temporal_network` where the committer branch referenced `git_graph` before it was defined. `transform_commit_message_id_to_network` was updated to build explicit nodes, fix a `stri_match_first_regex` call that was wrapping the matrix output in an unnecessary `data.table()` call, and compute edge weight as the count of commits linking each issue ID to each file.

For the depends pipeline, `transform_dependencies_to_network` was already following the correct pattern and required no changes.

### Model Graph Stage

The four constructors (`model_directed_graph`, `model_undirected_graph`, `model_bipartite_graph`, and `model_heterogeneous_graph`) are now purely thin wrappers. Each one takes a pre-built nodes table and edgelist table, wraps them in a named list, and assigns the appropriate S3 class. No logic lives in the constructors. All preparation is the responsibility of the transform.

### Projection Stage

`bipartite_graph_projection` and `temporal_graph_projection` are both S3 generics with dispatch methods for `bipartite_graph` and `heterogeneous_graph`. When a bipartite graph is projected, the result is reclassified as `undirected_graph`. When a temporal projection is performed, the result is reclassified as `directed_graph`. This reclassification means the export stage dispatches correctly without any action from the caller.

### Export Stage

`graph_to_dsmj` is an S3 generic with methods for all four graph types. The `is_directed` flag, which previously had to be passed explicitly by every caller, is now resolved internally by the method. `directed_graph`, `bipartite_graph`, and `heterogeneous_graph` all write edges once. `undirected_graph` doubles each edge by swapping src and dest per the DSMJ specification. `transform_dependencies_to_sdsmj` in dv8.R was updated to wrap the reshaped parse output in `model_directed_graph` before calling `graph_to_dsmj`, since S3 dispatch requires a classed object.

### Open Question

`graph_to_dsmj` requires a `label` column in the edgelist to drive the `dcast` that structures the DSMJ cell format. This column is currently added manually by the three DV8 convenience wrappers before calling the export function. Since DSMJ is a DV8-specific format, it is worth discussing whether this label requirement should be enforced at the export function boundary with a clear error message, or whether it should be documented as a precondition that callers are responsible for satisfying.

```sql
###### Github Commit Comments ######

#' Download Project Commit Comments
#'
#' Download commit comments from "GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/comments" endpoint.
#' These are comments left directly on a commit page on GitHub, outside of any pull request review.
#' The returned comment IDs match the \code{comment_id} field in the GHTorrent \code{commit_comments} table,
#' enabling sentiment label transfer by joining on comment ID.
#'
#' @param owner GitHub's repository owner (e.g. akka)
#' @param repo GitHub's repository name (e.g. akka-core)
#' @param token Your GitHub API token
#' @references For details, see \url{https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/comments?apiVersion=2022-11-28#list-commit-comments-for-a-repository}.
#' @export
github_api_project_commit_comments <- function(owner, repo, token){
  gh::gh("GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/comments",
         owner = owner,
         repo = repo,
         page = 1,
         per_page = 100,
         .token = token)
}
```
- `github_parse_project_commit_comments` - Parses commit comment API responses into a `data.table`
```sql
#' Parse Commit Comments JSON to Table
#'
#' Parses the response from \code{\link{github_api_project_commit_comments}} into a data.table.
#' Note not all columns available in the downloaded json are parsed.
#'
#' @param api_responses API response obtained from \code{\link{github_api_project_commit_comments}}.
#' @export
github_parse_project_commit_comments <- function(api_responses){
  parse_response <- function(api_response){
    parsed_response <- list()
    parsed_response[["comment_id"]] <- api_response[["id"]]
    parsed_response[["commit_id"]] <- api_response[["commit_id"]]
    parsed_response[["author_login"]] <- api_response[["user"]][["login"]]
    parsed_response[["author_id"]] <- api_response[["user"]][["id"]]
    parsed_response[["body"]] <- api_response[["body"]]
    parsed_response[["path"]] <- api_response[["path"]]
    parsed_response[["position"]] <- api_response[["position"]]
    parsed_response[["line"]] <- api_response[["line"]]
    parsed_response[["created_at"]] <- api_response[["created_at"]]
    parsed_response[["updated_at"]] <- api_response[["updated_at"]]

    parsed_response <- as.data.table(parsed_response)

    return(parsed_response)
  }
  rbindlist(lapply(api_responses, parse_response), fill = TRUE)
}
```
